clinicalPearls: Characterised by two coexisting features: transient, migratory erythematous patches that change shape over hours to days, and fixed, well-demarcated hyperkeratotic plaques
The migratory erythema can be provoked by temperature change, emotion and mechanical trauma
Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood, and the fixed plaques often favour the extensor limbs, buttocks and face
Most commonly autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in GJB3 (connexin 31) or GJB4 (connexin 30.3)
Palmoplantar keratoderma may be present in a proportion of cases
Sensation and general health are typically normal, distinguishing it from more severe ichthyoses
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics and oral retinoids for the fixed keratotic component, and avoidance of provoking factors
reference.pathophysiology: Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is most often an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in GJB3 or GJB4, which encode the gap-junction proteins connexin 31 and connexin 30.3. Connexins oligomerise into channels that permit direct exchange of ions and small signalling molecules between adjacent keratinocytes, coordinating epidermal differentiation and homeostasis. The mutations disturb assembly and function of these channels and may exert dominant-negative effects, disrupting intercellular communication in the epidermis. This produces two clinical components: labile vasomotor/erythematous change that migrates in response to stimuli, and abnormal terminal differentiation manifesting as fixed hyperkeratotic plaques.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis
Molecular genetic testing of GJB3 and GJB4
Clinical documentation/photography of the migratory erythema over time
Exclusion of inflammatory mimics where the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or generalised keratoderma causing functional impairment
Secondary infection of fissured hyperkeratotic plaques
Atypical features suggesting an alternative ichthyosis or syndrome
Significant psychosocial impact from visible, fluctuating erythema
reference.prognosis: Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is a chronic condition that tends to be stable or slowly progressive; the migratory erythema often lessens after childhood while the fixed plaques persist. General health and lifespan are normal, and oral retinoids can markedly improve the keratotic component.
pitfalls: Mistaking the migratory erythema for urticaria or an inflammatory dermatosis
Overlooking the coexistence of transient erythema and fixed plaques, which is the diagnostic hallmark
Assuming systemic or dangerous internal disease when general health is in fact preserved
Not counselling on trigger avoidance for the labile erythematous component
management: Oral retinoids (acitretin) as the mainstay for the fixed hyperkeratotic plaques, often producing marked improvement
Topical keratolytics and emollients to soften plaques and reduce scaling
Counsel avoidance of provoking stimuli such as temperature change, friction and emotional stress to limit the migratory erythema
Monitor patients on systemic retinoids for mucocutaneous, hepatic, lipid and skeletal effects, with teratogenicity precautions in women of childbearing potential
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant GJB3/GJB4 inheritance, with family assessment
Long-term dermatology follow-up given the chronic, slowly progressive course
